assignment.title: Algebra II Honors — Thanksgiving Break Packet
assignment.instructions: This packet reviews everything from the start of the year, one unit at a time. Each unit starts with the basics and builds up. When a question starts something new, read its notes and worked example first. You have 3 tries on each question, and hints are there when you need them.
assignment.teacherNotes: A cumulative review for students to work alone over Thanksgiving break: 11 units in the order they were taught, 72 questions, each unit running from its building block to grade level. Nearly every question is worked in a tool; units 9 and 10 (radical expressions and rational exponents) have no dedicated tool, so they use answer boxes that take one small step at a time, and sorts. The first question on each skill opens an authored worked example (a sibling problem with different numbers) and carries short guided notes. The last section is six audited Digital SAT questions on standards the packet reviews, so an Honors class meets its CCMR share with the file as it is.

sections.title: Unit 1 — Interval notation, domain and range

questions.prompt: Graph $-2 < x \le 6$ on the number line. Then write it in interval notation.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: A closed circle and a bracket mean the end is included (≤ or ≥). An open circle and a parenthesis mean it is not (< or >).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Graph 1 ≤ x < 4 and write it in interval notation. Closed circle at 1 → Open circle at 4 → Shade between 1 and 4 → [1, 4)

hints: Put one circle at −2 and one at 6. Which of them is included?
The symbol next to 6 is ≤, so 6 is included. The symbol next to −2 is <.
Write the smaller end first. Use a bracket for an included end and a parenthesis for an end that is left out.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. x ≤ 6 means that 6 is…

solutionReview.headline: One open end, one closed end.
reasoning: −2 < x: open circle at −2, because −2 is not included.
x ≤ 6: closed circle at 6, because 6 is included.
Shade between them and write the smaller end first: (−2, 6].
solutionReview.commonError: Writing [−2, 6): the bracket has to go with 6, the end that is included.

questions.prompt: Graph $x \ge -1$ on the number line. Then write it in interval notation.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: A graph that never ends goes to ∞ or −∞. Infinity is not a number, so it always gets a parenthesis.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Graph x < 3 and write it in interval notation. Open circle at 3 → Shade to the left, with an arrow → (−∞, 3)

hints: Is −1 included? Look at the symbol ≥.
Numbers greater than −1 are to the right of −1, and they never stop.
Start the interval at −1 and end it at ∞. Only −1 can have a bracket.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which way do you shade for x ≥ −1?

solutionReview.headline: A closed end and an arrow.
reasoning: Greater than −1 is to the right, so shade right with an arrow.
The interval starts at −1 and never ends: [−1, ∞).
solutionReview.commonError: Putting a bracket on ∞: infinity is never included, so it always gets a parenthesis.

questions.prompt: Graph $x < -3$ or $x \ge 2$ on the number line. Then write it in interval notation.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: “Or” means two separate pieces. Write each piece as its own interval and join them with ∪.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Graph x ≤ −1 or x > 4 and write it in interval notation. x ≤ −1: closed circle at −1, shade left → x > 4: open circle at 4, shade right → (−∞, −1] ∪ (4, ∞)

hints: Graph the two pieces one at a time. They do not touch.
x < −3 goes left from an open circle. x ≥ 2 goes right from a closed circle.
Write the left piece, then ∪, then the right piece.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. How many separate pieces does “x < −3 or x ≥ 2” have?

solutionReview.headline: Two rays joined by ∪.
reasoning: x < −3: open circle at −3, shade left. That piece is (−∞, −3).
x ≥ 2: closed circle at 2, shade right. That piece is [2, ∞).
solutionReview.commonError: Shading between −3 and 2: “or” keeps the two outside pieces, not the middle.

questions.prompt: Show the relation {(−2, 3), (0, 5), (1, 3), (4, −1)} as a mapping and as a graph. Then state its domain and range, and decide whether it is a function.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: The domain is the set of inputs (x-values) and the range is the set of outputs (y-values). A relation is a function when every input has exactly one output.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: For the relation {(1, 2), (3, 2), (3, 5)}, state the domain and range and decide whether it is a function. Arrows: 1 → 2, 3 → 2, 3 → 5 → Domain: {1, 3} → Range: {2, 5} → Not a function

hints: Each ordered pair is (input, output). Draw one arrow for each pair.
List each input once for the domain, and each output once for the range.
Look at the inputs. Does any input have two different outputs?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In the ordered pair (4, −1), the input is…

solutionReview.headline: Inputs, outputs, then one output for each input.
reasoning: The inputs are −2, 0, 1 and 4, so the domain is {−2, 0, 1, 4}.
The outputs are 3, 5, 3 and −1. List 3 only once: the range is {−1, 3, 5}.
No input is used twice, so every input has exactly one output: it is a function.
Two inputs share the output 3. That is allowed in a function.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Domain {−2, 0, 1, 4}; range {−1, 3, 5}; it is a function
solutionReview.commonError: Saying it is not a function because the output 3 appears twice: a function may repeat an output, but not an input.

questions.prompt: The graph of $f(x) = -x + 3$ is drawn only for $-2 \le x < 5$. State its domain and range in interval notation.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Domain: every x the graph uses, read left to right. Range: every y the graph reaches, read bottom to top.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: The graph of f(x) = x + 1 is drawn only for −3 < x ≤ 2. State the domain and range. Domain: read left to right, from x = −3 to x = 2 → Domain: (−3, 2] → Range: the lowest y is f(−3) = −2 and the highest is f(2) = 3 → Range: (−2, 3]

hints: For the domain, look left to right. Where does the graph start and stop?
For the range, find the height of each end: f(−2) and f(5).
This line goes down, so the closed circle is the highest point. Write the lowest y first.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The domain of a graph is read…
options: left to right, along the x-axis
bottom to top, along the y-axis
scaffold.correct: left to right, along the x-axis

solutionReview.headline: Read x left to right, then y bottom to top.
reasoning: Domain: x runs from −2 (closed circle) to 5 (open circle): [−2, 5).
The ends are f(−2) = 5 (closed circle) and f(5) = −2 (open circle).
Range: y runs from −2 up to 5, and the closed end is the top: (−2, 5].
solutionReview.commonError: Copying the domain’s brackets onto the range: this line falls, so the closed end is the highest y, not the lowest.

questions.prompt: Use the graph of $f(x) = -|x - 1| + 4$. State where $f$ is increasing, decreasing, positive and negative.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Increasing and decreasing change at the vertex. Positive and negative change at the x-intercepts. All four answers are intervals of x.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: For f(x) = |x + 1| − 2, state where f is increasing, decreasing, positive and negative. The vertex is (−1, −2) and the V opens up → Decreasing on (−∞, −1); increasing on (−1, ∞) → x-intercepts: |x + 1| = 2, so x = −3 and x = 1 → Negative on (−3, 1) → Positive on (−∞, −3) ∪ (1, ∞)

hints: Find the vertex first. The graph rises on one side of it and falls on the other.
Find where the graph crosses the x-axis. Above the axis is positive; below it is negative.
Every answer uses x-values with parentheses: the turning point and the crossing points are not included.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. “f is positive” means the graph is…

solutionReview.headline: Vertex for up and down; x-intercepts for the sign.
reasoning: The vertex is (1, 4) and the V opens down: increasing on (−∞, 1), decreasing on (1, ∞).
x-intercepts: −|x − 1| + 4 = 0 gives |x − 1| = 4, so x = −3 and x = 5.
The graph is above the x-axis between them: positive on (−3, 5).
It is below the axis outside them: negative on (−∞, −3) ∪ (5, ∞).
solutionReview.commonError: Answering “positive” with where the graph is rising: positive means above the x-axis, wherever the graph is heading.

questions.prompt: Analyze the parent function $f(x) = x^2$. State its domain, its range and its vertex.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: A parent function is the simplest graph of its family. Know its shape, its turning point, and which x- and y-values it uses.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: For the parent function f(x) = |x|, state the domain, the range and the vertex. Vertex: (0, 0) → Domain: (−∞, ∞) → Range: [0, ∞)

hints: The vertex is the point where the parabola turns around.
Can you square any number? That tells you the domain.
A square is never negative. What is the smallest value x² can be?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Can x² ever be a negative number?

solutionReview.headline: The parabola turns at the origin.
reasoning: The vertex is (0, 0), where the graph turns around.
Any number can be squared, so the domain is (−∞, ∞).
x² is never negative and equals 0 at the vertex, so the range is [0, ∞).
solutionReview.commonError: Giving the range as (−∞, ∞): the parabola never goes below its vertex.

questions.prompt: Analyze the parent function $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$. State its domain, its range and where it is increasing.
hints: Which numbers have a real square root? That is the domain.
The graph starts at a point and goes one way only. Find the starting point.
From its starting point, does the graph ever go down?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Is √(−4) a real number?

solutionReview.headline: The graph starts at the origin and only rises.
reasoning: Only x ≥ 0 has a real square root, so the domain is [0, ∞).
The outputs start at √0 = 0 and grow without end, so the range is [0, ∞).
The graph rises all the way from its starting point, so f increases over its whole domain, from 0 on.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Domain [0, ∞); range [0, ∞); increasing from x = 0 on
solutionReview.commonError: Writing the domain as (−∞, ∞): negative numbers have no real square root.

questions.prompt: The graph shows $y = x^2$ after it was moved. Find $a$, $h$ and $k$ in $y = a(x - h)^2 + k$.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: In y = a·f(x − h) + k, the point (0, 0) of the parent moves to (h, k). a stretches or flips the graph.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: A graph of y = a(x − h)² + k has its vertex at (−1, 4) and passes through (0, 6). Find a, h and k. h = −1 and k = 4 → From the vertex, 1 step right is 2 steps up → a = 2 → y = 2(x + 1)² + 4

hints: Find the vertex of the graph. Its coordinates are (h, k).
Go one step right from the vertex. How far up or down does the graph go? That is a.
A vertex to the right of the y-axis has a positive h, and the equation then shows x minus that number.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The vertex of y = a(x − h)² + k is the point…

solutionReview.headline: Read the vertex, then one step from it.
reasoning: The vertex is (3, −2), so h = 3 and k = −2.
One step right of the vertex the graph is 1 unit higher, the same as y = x², so a = 1.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing h = −3 because the equation shows x − 3: the form is x − h, so h is 3.

questions.prompt: Describe every transformation that takes $y = \sqrt{x}$ to $g(x) = 2\sqrt{x + 1} - 4$.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Read one number at a time. Outside numbers (a and k) act on y as they look. The inside number (h) acts on x in the opposite direction.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Describe how the graph of y = x² becomes g(x) = −3(x − 2)² + 1. a = −3 is negative: reflect across the x-axis → |a| = 3: vertical stretch by a factor of 3 → Nothing multiplies x inside: no horizontal stretch, no reflection across the y-axis → x − 2 inside: 2 units right → + 1 outside: 1 unit up

hints: The 2 in front multiplies every y-value. Is it negative? Is its size more than 1?
x + 1 is inside the root. Inside changes move the graph the opposite way. Nothing multiplies x, so there is no horizontal stretch and no reflection across the y-axis.
The −4 at the end is outside. It moves the graph down.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which way does x + 1 inside the root move the graph?

solutionReview.headline: a, then h, then k.
reasoning: a = 2 is positive, so there is no reflection across the x-axis. It is a vertical stretch by a factor of 2.
Nothing multiplies x inside the root: the horizontal scale is unchanged (factor 1) and there is no reflection across the y-axis.
x + 1 means h = −1: the graph moves 1 unit left.
k = −4: the graph moves 4 units down.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Vertical stretch by 2, left 1, down 4, no reflection
solutionReview.commonError: Moving the graph right 1 because of the plus sign: inside the function, + moves left.

questions.prompt: The point $(2, 4)$ is on $y = x^2$. Find where it lands on $y = -(x - 3)^2 + 2$.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Every point (x, y) of the parent moves to (x + h, a·y + k): shift x by h, multiply y by a, then add k.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: The point (4, 2) is on y = √x. Where does it land on y = 3√(x + 1) − 5? h = −1, so new x = 4 − 1 = 3 → a = 3, so y becomes 3 · 2 = 6 → k = −5, so new y = 6 − 5 = 1 → (4, 2) → (3, 1)

hints: Work on x and y separately. Only h changes x.
x − 3 moves the point 3 to the right.
For y: multiply the old y by a first, then add k.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In y = −(x − 3)² + 2, the value of a is…

solutionReview.headline: (x, y) → (x + h, a·y + k).
solutionReview.commonError: Adding k before multiplying by a: multiply the y-value by a first, then add k.

questions.prompt: The dashed graph is $y = x^3$ after transformations. Change $a$, $h$ and $k$ until your graph matches it.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Find where the parent’s center point (0, 0) went: that is (h, k). Then use one more point to find a.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: A dashed graph is y = x³ moved and stretched. Its center point is (−2, 1), and one step right of the center it is 3 units higher. Find a, h and k. h = −2 and k = 1 → One step right of the center, the graph is 3 higher → a = 3 → y = 3(x + 2)³ + 1

hints: Find the center of the dashed curve, the point where it bends from one direction to the other.
Set h and k to that point first, so the two centers sit on top of each other.
Does the dashed graph rise or fall to the right? A graph of x³ that falls to the right has a negative a.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The graph of y = −x³ goes which way as you move right?

solutionReview.headline: Center first, then direction.
reasoning: The center of the dashed graph is (2, 1), so h = 2 and k = 1.
One step right of the center the dashed graph is 1 unit lower, so a = −1.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving a = 1: the dashed graph falls to the right, so it has been reflected and a is negative.

sections.title: Unit 3 — Inverses, operations on functions and composition

questions.prompt: Send $x = 3$ through $f(x) = 2x + 1$. Then undo it with the inverse to find $f^{-1}(f(3))$.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: An inverse function undoes the function: it takes each output back to the input it came from.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: f(x) = x + 6. Send x = 2 through f, then through the inverse of f. f(2) = 2 + 6 = 8 → The inverse subtracts 6 → f⁻¹(8) = 8 − 6 = 2 → f⁻¹(f(2)) = 2

hints: First find the output of f: double the input, then add 1.
The inverse undoes those two steps in reverse order: subtract 1, then divide by 2.
A function followed by its inverse returns the number you started with.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What undoes “multiply by 2”?

solutionReview.headline: Out with f, back with the inverse.
reasoning: The inverse undoes f: subtract 1, then divide by 2. (7 − 1) ÷ 2 = 3.
So the inverse brings 7 back to 3, the starting number.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping at f(3) = 7: the question asks for the value after the inverse has undone f.

questions.prompt: Find the inverse of $f(x) = 3x - 6$. Swap $x$ and $y$, then solve for $y$.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: To find an inverse rule: write y for f(x), swap x and y, then solve for y.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Find the inverse of f(x) = 2x + 8. y = 2x + 8 → x = 2y + 8 → x − 8 = 2y → (x − 8)/2 = y, so y = x/2 − 4 → f⁻¹(x) = x/2 − 4

hints: Start from y = 3x − 6 and swap the letters: x = 3y − 6.
To get y alone, undo the −6 first.
Then undo the multiplication by 3. Divide every term on the other side.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. After swapping x and y in y = 3x − 6, the equation is…

solutionReview.headline: Swap, then solve for y.
reasoning: Divide both sides by 3: y = (x + 6)/3 = x/3 + 2.
Check with a number: f(4) = 6, and 6/3 + 2 = 4.
solutionReview.commonError: Dividing only x by 3 and leaving the 6: every term on that side is divided by 3.

questions.prompt: Find the inverse of $f(x) = -5x + 15$. Swap $x$ and $y$, then solve for $y$.
hints: Swap first: x = −5y + 15.
Subtract 15 from both sides, so the y-term is alone.
Divide both sides by −5. Dividing by a negative changes the sign of every term.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is 15 ÷ (−5)?

solutionReview.headline: Swap, subtract 15, divide by −5.
reasoning: Check with a number: f(2) = 5, and −5/5 + 3 = 2.
solutionReview.commonError: Losing a sign when dividing by −5: both x and −15 change sign.

questions.prompt: Let $f(x) = 2x^2 + 3x - 1$ and $g(x) = x^2 - 5x + 4$. Find $(f + g)(x)$ by adding like terms.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: (f + g)(x) means f(x) + g(x). Add the two rules by combining like terms.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: f(x) = x² + 4x and g(x) = 3x² − x + 2. Find (f + g)(x). (x² + 4x) + (3x² − x + 2) → x² + 3x² = 4x² → 4x + (−x) = 3x → (f + g)(x) = 4x² + 3x + 2

hints: Line up the like terms: x² with x², x with x, number with number.
Add the coefficients in each column. The exponents do not change.
Watch the signs: 3x + (−5x) is negative.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which pair are like terms?

solutionReview.headline: Add column by column.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding the exponents: 2x² + x² is 3x², not 3x⁴.

questions.prompt: Let $f(x) = x + 3$ and $g(x) = 2x - 5$. Find $(f \cdot g)(x)$ with the area model.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: (f · g)(x) means f(x) times g(x). Multiply every term of one rule by every term of the other, then combine like terms.

hints: The model has four cells. Each cell is one term of x + 3 times one term of 2x − 5.
x · 2x = 2x². Keep the minus sign with the 5.
Two of the cells are x terms. Combine them for the middle term.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is x · 2x?

solutionReview.headline: Four cells, then combine.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying only the first terms and the last terms: the two middle cells make the x term.

questions.prompt: Let $f(x) = 3x - 1$ and $g(x) = x + 4$. Find $(f \circ g)(2)$ and $(g \circ f)(2)$.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: (f ∘ g)(x) means f(g(x)): work from the inside out. The output of the inside function is the input of the outside one.

hints: (f ∘ g)(2) is f(g(2)). Find g(2) first.
Put that answer into f.
For (g ∘ f)(2), switch the order: find f(2) first, then put it into g.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In f(g(2)), which function is used first?

solutionReview.headline: Inside first, both ways.
reasoning: The two orders give different answers.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying f(2) by g(2): composition puts one function inside the other, it does not multiply them.

questions.prompt: Let $f(x) = 2x - 3$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 1$. Find the rules for $f(g(x))$ and $g(f(x))$, one step at a time.

responses.label: f(g(x)): put x² + 1 in place of x in 2x − 3. Before simplifying, 2(x² + 1) − 3 = 2x² + 2 − 3. Simplified, f(g(x)) =

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: To compose two rules, replace every x in the outside function with the whole inside rule, in parentheses. Then simplify.

hints: For f(g(x)), the inside rule x² + 1 takes the place of x in 2x − 3.
(2x − 3)² means (2x − 3)(2x − 3). It has a middle term.
For g(f(x)), square 2x − 3 first, then add the 1 from g.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. f(g(x)) means…

solutionReview.headline: Substitute the whole rule, then simplify.
solutionReview.commonError: Squaring 2x − 3 as 4x² + 9: (2x − 3)² also has the middle term −12x.

sections.title: Unit 4 — Absolute value: graphs, equations and inequalities

questions.prompt: The graph shows $y = |x|$ after it was moved. Find $a$, $h$ and $k$ in $y = a|x - h| + k$.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: The vertex of y = a|x − h| + k is the point (h, k). a tells how steep the V is and whether it opens up or down.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: A V-shaped graph of y = a|x − h| + k has its vertex at (4, −1) and opens up with slopes 1 and −1. Find a, h and k. h = 4 and k = −1 → One step right of the vertex, the graph is 1 unit higher → a = 1 → y = |x − 4| − 1

hints: Find the point of the V. Its coordinates are (h, k).
A vertex to the left of the y-axis has a negative h.
Go one step right from the vertex. The change in height is a.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The vertex of y = |x| is at…

solutionReview.headline: Read the vertex, then the steepness.
reasoning: The vertex is (−3, 2), so h = −3 and k = 2.
One step right of the vertex the graph is 1 unit higher, so a = 1.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing h = 3 because the equation shows x + 3: x + 3 is x − (−3), so h is −3.

questions.prompt: The graph of $f(x) = |x|$ is shown with five points. Graph $g(x) = 2|x - 1| - 3$ by moving each point to its new place.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: For g(x) = a|x − h| + k, each point (x, y) of |x| moves to (x + h, a·y + k).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Graph g(x) = −|x + 2| + 4 by moving the points (−1, 1), (0, 0) and (1, 1) of f(x) = |x|. Rule: (x, y) → (x − 2, −y + 4) → (0, 0) → (−2, 4) → (−1, 1) → (−3, 3) → (1, 1) → (−1, 3) → The new V has its vertex at (−2, 4) and opens down

hints: Start with the vertex of f. It moves to the vertex of g, the point (h, k).
For every point, x shifts the way the number inside the bars says: the opposite of its sign.
For every point, multiply the old y by the number in front of the bars, then add the number at the end.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which way does x − 1 inside the bars move the graph?

solutionReview.headline: Move each point with (x, y) → (x + 1, 2y − 3).
reasoning: g is twice as steep as f, shifted right 1 and down 3.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Vertex (1, −3); the other points are (0, −1), (2, −1), (−1, 1) and (3, 1)
solutionReview.commonError: Subtracting 3 before multiplying by 2: multiply the y-value by 2 first.

questions.prompt: Solve $|x - 3| = 5$. Split it into two equations and check both answers.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: |A| = d means A is d units from zero, so A = d or A = −d. Most absolute value equations have two answers.

hints: What two numbers have an absolute value of 5?
Write two equations: the inside equals the positive number, or the inside equals the negative number.
Solve each equation by adding 3 to both sides.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which numbers are 5 units from zero?

solutionReview.headline: Split, solve, check.
reasoning: The bars are alone, so split: x − 3 = 5 or x − 3 = −5.
Add 3 in each: x = 8 or x = −2.
solutionReview.commonError: Solving only x − 3 = 5: the inside can also equal −5.

questions.prompt: Solve $2|x + 1| - 3 = 7$. Get the absolute value alone first, then split.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Get the bars alone before you split: undo what is added or subtracted, then what is multiplied.

hints: Undo the −3 first: add 3 to both sides.
Then divide both sides by 2, so the bars are alone.
Now split into two equations and solve each one.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is the first move in 2|x + 1| − 3 = 7?

solutionReview.headline: Isolate, split, solve, check.
reasoning: Split: x + 1 = 5 or x + 1 = −5, so x = 4 or x = −6.
solutionReview.commonError: Splitting before the bars are alone, as 2(x + 1) − 3 = −7: isolate the absolute value first.

questions.prompt: A refrigerator is set to 37°F. Its warmest and coldest temperatures are 3 degrees away from that setting. Write and solve an absolute value equation for those two temperatures $T$.

responses.label: How far from the setting, in degrees
An absolute value equation for the two temperatures T

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: |x − center| = distance says “x is exactly that distance from the center.”

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: A bolt should be 60 mm long. The longest and shortest bolts allowed are 2 mm away from that. Write an absolute value equation for those two lengths L. Center: 60 → Distance: 2 → |L − 60| = 2 → L = 62 or L = 58

hints: The setting is the center. The number of degrees it can be off by is the distance.
The distance between T and the setting is written |T − setting|.
To find the two temperatures, go that distance below the setting and the same distance above it.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. |T − 37| stands for…

solutionReview.headline: Center inside the bars, distance on the other side.
reasoning: The center is 37 and the distance is 3.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing |T − 3| = 37: the center goes inside the bars and the distance goes on the other side.

questions.prompt: Solve $|x + 1| < 4$. Then graph the solution and write it in interval notation.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: |A| < d means A is close to zero: −d < A < d. The answer is one piece, between two numbers.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Solve |x − 2| ≤ 3. Graph the solution and write it in interval notation. −3 ≤ x − 2 ≤ 3 → −1 ≤ x ≤ 5 → Closed circles at −1 and 5, shaded between → [−1, 5]

hints: “Less than” means the inside is between −4 and 4.
Write −4 < x + 1 < 4, then subtract 1 from all three parts.
The symbol is <, so the circles are open and the interval uses parentheses.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. |A| < 4 means A is…

solutionReview.headline: Less than means between.
reasoning: Write it as a between statement: −4 < x + 1 < 4.
Subtract 1 from all three parts: −5 < x < 3.
Open circles at −5 and 3, shaded between: (−5, 3).
solutionReview.commonError: Solving only x + 1 < 4: the inside must also be greater than −4.

questions.prompt: Solve $|x - 4| > 2$. Then graph the solution and write it in interval notation.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: |A| > d means A is far from zero: A < −d or A > d. The answer is two outside pieces.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Solve |x + 3| ≥ 1. Graph the solution and write it in interval notation. x + 3 ≤ −1 or x + 3 ≥ 1 → x ≤ −4 or x ≥ −2 → Closed circles at −4 and −2, shaded outward → (−∞, −4] ∪ [−2, ∞)

hints: “Greater than” means the inside is below −2 or above 2.
Write two inequalities: x − 4 < −2 or x − 4 > 2. Add 4 in each.
The graph has two pieces that point away from each other. Join the intervals with ∪.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. |A| > 2 means A is…

solutionReview.headline: Greater than means outside.
reasoning: Write two inequalities: x − 4 < −2 or x − 4 > 2.
Add 4 in each: x < 2 or x > 6.
Open circles at 2 and 6, shaded outward: (−∞, 2) ∪ (6, ∞).
solutionReview.commonError: Writing 2 < x < 6: that is the “less than” answer. Greater than gives the two outside pieces.

questions.prompt: Solve $-3|x + 2| + 5 \ge -4$. Then graph the solution and write it in interval notation.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Isolate the bars first. When you multiply or divide an inequality by a negative number, reverse the symbol.

hints: Subtract 5 from both sides first.
Divide both sides by −3. What happens to ≥ when you divide by a negative number?
After the symbol reverses you have a “less than or equal to”: the inside is between two numbers.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What happens to ≥ when you divide both sides by −3?

solutionReview.headline: Isolate, reverse the symbol, then “between”.
reasoning: Divide by −3 and reverse the symbol: |x + 2| ≤ 3.
Closed circles at −5 and 1, shaded between: [−5, 1].
solutionReview.commonError: Not reversing the symbol when dividing by −3, which gives the two outside pieces instead.

questions.prompt: Solve the system $2x + y = 11$ and $x - y = 1$ by elimination. Check your ordered pair in both equations.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Elimination: add or subtract the equations so one variable cancels. Solve for the other, then substitute back.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Solve x + y = 9 and x − y = 5 by elimination. (x + y) + (x − y) = 9 + 5 → 2x = 14, so x = 7 → 7 + y = 9, so y = 2 → 7 + 2 = 9 and 7 − 2 = 5

hints: Look at the y-terms: +y and −y. What happens if you add the two equations?
After adding, only x is left. Solve for x.
Put your x into either equation to find y.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is y + (−y)?

solutionReview.headline: Add the equations to cancel y.
reasoning: Substitute into x − y = 1: 4 − y = 1, so y = 3.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping after finding x: a solution of a system needs a value for every variable.

questions.prompt: Solve the system $x + y + z = 6$, $x - y + z = 2$ and $x + y - z = 0$ by elimination. Eliminate the same variable from two pairs of equations, then check your ordered triple.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Eliminate the same variable twice, with two different pairs of equations. That leaves a smaller system in two variables.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Solve x + y + z = 9, x − y + z = 3 and x + y − z = 1. Equation 1 + equation 2: 2x + 2z = 12 → Equation 2 + equation 3: 2x = 4 → x = 2, then 2(2) + 2z = 12 gives z = 4 → 2 + y + 4 = 9, so y = 3 → (2, 3, 4): 2 + 3 + 4 = 9, 2 − 3 + 4 = 3, 2 + 3 − 4 = 1

hints: Add equations 1 and 2. Which variable cancels?
Now add equations 2 and 3. The same variable cancels again.
Solve the smaller system, then put those values into an original equation for the last variable.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. To get a 2×2 system, the two pairs must eliminate…

solutionReview.headline: Eliminate y twice, then back-substitute.
reasoning: Equation 1: 1 + y + 3 = 6, so y = 2. The triple (1, 2, 3) checks in all three equations.
solutionReview.commonError: Eliminating y from one pair and z from the other: the two new equations must have the same two variables.

questions.prompt: Solve the system $x + 2y - z = 4$, $2x - y + z = 6$ and $x + y + 2z = 6$ by elimination. One pair needs an equation multiplied first. Check your ordered triple.
hints: Equations 1 and 2 have −z and +z. Add them to eliminate z.
To eliminate z from equations 2 and 3, multiply equation 2 by 2 first, then subtract equation 3.
You now have two equations in x and y. Solve them, then find z.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. To cancel +z against +2z, you can multiply the first of those equations by…

solutionReview.headline: Eliminate z twice, scaling one equation.
reasoning: 2 × equation 2 − equation 3: 3x − 3y = 6, which is x − y = 2.
Add those two: 4x = 12, so x = 3 and y = 1.
Equation 2: 2(3) − 1 + z = 6, so z = 1. The triple (3, 1, 1) checks in all three equations.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying only part of an equation: when you scale an equation, every term is multiplied, the constant too.

questions.prompt: Matrix A shows how many granola bars and smoothies two friends bought. Matrix B shows the price of each. Multiply $A \cdot B$ to find what each friend paid.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: To multiply matrices, pair a row of the first with a column of the second: multiply the matching numbers and add.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: A has rows [2 1] and [0 3]. B is the column with 4 on top and 5 below. Find A · B. A is 2 × 2 and B is 2 × 1 → Row 1: 2(4) + 1(5) = 13 → Row 2: 0(4) + 3(5) = 15 → A · B is the column with 13 on top and 15 below

hints: For Ana, use row 1 of A: 3 bars and 2 smoothies.
Multiply each count by its price, then add the two products.
Do the same for Ben with row 2 of A.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. 3 bars at $2 each cost…

solutionReview.headline: Row times column, for each friend.
reasoning: A is 2 × 2 and B is 2 × 1, so the product is 2 × 1: one total for each friend.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding the counts and prices instead of multiplying: each count is multiplied by its price before the products are added.

questions.prompt: Write the system $x + 2y - z = 4$, $3x - y = 5$ and $2x + y + 2z = 9$ as a matrix equation $A \cdot X = B$. Fill in the coefficient matrix, the variable matrix and the constant matrix.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: A holds the coefficients, X the variables, B the constants. A missing variable has coefficient 0, and a variable with no number has coefficient 1 or −1.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Write 2x + y − z = 3, x + 4z = 9 and 3x − 2y + z = 4 as a matrix equation A · X = B. Row 1 of A: 2, 1, −1 → Row 2 of A: 1, 0, 4 → Row 3 of A: 3, −2, 1 → X is the column x, y, z → B is the column 3, 9, 4

hints: Each row of A is one equation: the numbers in front of x, y and z, in that order.
The second equation has no z. What number goes in its z place?
−z has coefficient −1, and x alone has coefficient 1.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In 3x − y = 5, the coefficient of z is…

solutionReview.headline: Coefficients, variables, constants.
reasoning: Row 1 of A is 1, 2, −1. Row 2 is 3, −1, 0. Row 3 is 2, 1, 2.
X is the column x, y, z.
solutionReview.answerSummary: A has rows [1 2 −1], [3 −1 0], [2 1 2]; X is the column x, y, z; B is the column 4, 5, 9
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving the missing z out of row 2: every row needs three entries, so a missing variable is 0.

questions.prompt: Solve the system $x + y + z = 10$, $2x - y + z = 6$ and $x + 2y - z = 3$ with matrices. Write $A \cdot X = B$, then use the calculator to find $X = A^{-1} \cdot B$.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: To solve A · X = B, multiply by the inverse of A: X = A⁻¹ · B. The calculator does the arithmetic; you set up A and B.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Solve x + y + z = 6, 2x − y + z = 3 and x + 2y − z = 2 with matrices. A has rows [1 1 1], [2 −1 1] and [1 2 −1] → B is the column 6, 3, 2 → X = A⁻¹ · B → The calculator gives the column 1, 2, 3 → (1, 2, 3): 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, 2 − 2 + 3 = 3, 1 + 4 − 3 = 2

hints: Enter the coefficients row by row. −y and −z have coefficient −1.
B is the column of constants: the numbers after the equal signs.
Run A⁻¹ · B and read x, y and z from top to bottom.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which matrix holds the numbers after the equal signs?

solutionReview.headline: Set up A and B, then X = A⁻¹ · B.
reasoning: A has rows [1 1 1], [2 −1 1] and [1 2 −1]. B is the column 10, 6, 3.
solutionReview.commonError: Entering −y as 1 instead of −1: the sign belongs to the coefficient.

questions.prompt: A snack stand sold 30 items for $64: waters at $1, bags of chips at $2 and sandwiches at $5. It sold 4 more waters than chips and sandwiches together. Let x, y and z be the numbers of waters, chips and sandwiches. Write a matrix equation that models the situation, and solve it.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Each fact in the story is one equation: a total count, a total amount of money, and a comparison. Put the variables on one side before you fill in the matrix.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: A theater sold 20 tickets for $88: child tickets at $2, student tickets at $4 and adult tickets at $6. It sold twice as many student tickets as child tickets. How many of each? c = child, s = student, a = adult tickets → c + s + a = 20 → 2c + 4s + 6a = 88 → s = 2c, or −2c + s = 0 → Solve A · X = B: c = 4, s = 8, a = 8

hints: First fact: the three counts add to 30.
Second fact: each price times its count adds to 64.
Third fact: x = y + z + 4. Move y and z to the left side before you write the row.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. “30 items in all” becomes the equation…

solutionReview.headline: Three facts, three equations.
reasoning: Count: x + y + z = 30. Money: x + 2y + 5z = 64.
Comparison: x = y + z + 4, which is x − y − z = 4.
A has rows [1 1 1], [1 2 5] and [1 −1 −1]. B is the column 30, 64, 4.
solutionReview.answerSummary: 17 waters, 6 bags of chips and 7 sandwiches
solutionReview.commonError: Writing the comparison row as 1, 1, 1 with constant 4: after moving y and z to the left, their coefficients are −1.

questions.prompt: Simplify $(3x^2 + 2x - 5) + (x^2 - 6x + 1)$. Line up the like terms and add.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Like terms have the same variable and the same exponent. To add them, add the coefficients and keep the exponent.

hints: Which terms go in the same column? Match the exponents.
x² means 1x². Add the coefficients in each column.
Watch the signs: 2x + (−6x) is negative.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. 3x² + x² equals…

solutionReview.headline: Add column by column.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding the exponents as well as the coefficients: only the coefficients are added.

questions.prompt: Simplify $(5x^2 - 2x + 7) - (2x^2 + 4x - 3)$. Write the opposite of every term of the second polynomial, then add.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Subtracting a polynomial means adding its opposite: change the sign of every term in the second polynomial, then add.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Simplify (4x² + 3x − 2) − (x² − 5x + 6). The opposite of x² − 5x + 6 is −x² + 5x − 6 → 4x² + (−x²) = 3x² → 3x + 5x = 8x → −2 + (−6) = −8 → 3x² + 8x − 8

hints: The minus sign in front changes every term inside the second parentheses, not only the first.
The opposite of −3 is +3. What are the opposites of 2x² and 4x?
Now add each column: −2x and the opposite of 4x are both negative.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The opposite of −3 is…

solutionReview.headline: Change every sign, then add.
reasoning: The opposites of 2x², 4x and −3 are −2x², −4x and 3.
solutionReview.commonError: Changing only the first sign: −(2x² + 4x − 3) changes all three terms, so the −3 becomes +3.

questions.prompt: Simplify $3x(2x^2 - x + 4)$ with the area model. Fill in every cell, then write the product.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Distribute: multiply the outside term by every term inside. Multiply the coefficients and add the exponents.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Simplify −2x(x² + 3x − 5). −2x · x² = −2x³ → −2x · 3x = −6x² → −2x · (−5) = 10x → −2x³ − 6x² + 10x

hints: Each cell is 3x times one term of 2x² − x + 4.
3x · 2x²: multiply 3 by 2, and add the exponents of x.
−x means −1x, so its product with 3x is negative.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. x · x² equals…

solutionReview.headline: One row, three cells.
reasoning: No two cells are like terms, so the product is their sum.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying the exponents: x · x² is x³, because the exponents are added.

questions.prompt: Simplify $(2x - 3)(x + 5)$ with the area model. Fill in every cell, then combine like terms.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Two binomials make four products. Two of them are like terms, so they combine into the middle term.

hints: There are four cells: each term of 2x − 3 times each term of x + 5.
Keep the minus sign with the 3 in every product.
Two cells are x terms. Add them for the middle term.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. −3 · 5 equals…

solutionReview.headline: Four cells, then combine.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing 2x² − 15 only: the two middle cells, 10x and −3x, are part of the product.

questions.prompt: Simplify $(x - 2)(x^2 + 3x - 4)$ with the area model. Fill in every cell, then combine like terms.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Every term of the first factor multiplies every term of the second: 2 terms times 3 terms is 6 cells. Then combine like terms.

hints: There are six cells. Start with the row for x.
In the row for −2, every product changes sign.
Look for cells with the same power of x: there is a pair of x² terms and a pair of x terms.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. How many cells does a 2-term by 3-term area model have?

solutionReview.headline: Six cells, two pairs of like terms.
solutionReview.commonError: Losing the sign in the −2 row: −2 · (−4) is +8.

sections.title: Unit 7 — Dividing polynomials; the Remainder and Factor Theorems

questions.prompt: Use long division to find $(x^2 + 7x + 10) \div (x + 2)$.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Long division repeats four moves: divide the leading terms, multiply back, subtract, bring down.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Divide (x² + 6x + 8) ÷ (x + 2) by long division. x² ÷ x = x → x(x + 2) = x² + 2x → (x² + 6x) − (x² + 2x) = 4x; bring down 8 → 4x ÷ x = 4, and 4(x + 2) = 4x + 8 → (4x + 8) − (4x + 8) = 0 → Quotient x + 4, remainder 0

hints: Start with the leading terms: x² ÷ x.
Multiply your answer by the whole divisor, x + 2, and subtract it.
Bring down the 10 and repeat with the new leading term.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is x² ÷ x?

solutionReview.headline: Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.
reasoning: x² ÷ x = x, and x(x + 2) = x² + 2x.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying back by only the x of the divisor: the new term multiplies the whole divisor, x + 2.

questions.prompt: Use long division to find $(2x^2 + 3x - 4) \div (x - 2)$. This one has a remainder.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: When the last subtraction does not leave 0, what is left is the remainder. Subtracting a negative term adds it.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Divide (3x² − 5x + 1) ÷ (x − 1) by long division. 3x² ÷ x = 3x, and 3x(x − 1) = 3x² − 3x → (3x² − 5x) − (3x² − 3x) = −2x; bring down 1 → −2x ÷ x = −2, and −2(x − 1) = −2x + 2 → (−2x + 1) − (−2x + 2) = −1 → Quotient 3x − 2, remainder −1

hints: 2x² ÷ x gives the first term of the quotient.
When you subtract 2x² − 4x, the −4x becomes +4x: 3x + 4x.
Keep going until what is left has no x. That number is the remainder.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. 3x − (−4x) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Two rounds, then a remainder.
solutionReview.commonError: Subtracting −4x as if it were +4x, which gives −x: subtracting a negative adds.

questions.prompt: Use long division to find $(6x^2 + 5x - 4) \div (2x - 1)$.
hints: Divide the leading terms: 6x² ÷ 2x. Divide the numbers and the letters.
Multiply that term by 2x − 1 and subtract. Subtracting −3x adds 3x.
Repeat with the new leading term. This division comes out even.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is 6x² ÷ 2x?

solutionReview.headline: The divisor starts with 2x, so divide by 2x each round.
solutionReview.commonError: Dividing 6x² by x instead of by 2x: use the whole leading term of the divisor.

questions.prompt: Use synthetic division to find $(x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6) \div (x - 3)$.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Synthetic division is a shortcut for dividing by x − r. It uses only the coefficients: bring down, multiply by r, add.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Divide (x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6) ÷ (x − 2) by synthetic division. r = 2; coefficients 1, 2, −5, −6 → Bring down 1 → 1 · 2 = 2, and 2 + 2 = 4 → 4 · 2 = 8, and −5 + 8 = 3 → 3 · 2 = 6, and −6 + 6 = 0 → Quotient x² + 4x + 3, remainder 0

hints: The number in the corner makes the divisor zero: x − 3 = 0.
Bring the first coefficient down. Multiply it by r and write the product under the next coefficient.
Add each column. The last sum is the remainder; the others are the quotient’s coefficients.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For the divisor x − 3, the number in the corner is…

solutionReview.headline: Bring down, multiply by 3, add.
reasoning: The bottom row 1, 1, −2 gives the quotient x² + x − 2, and the remainder is 0.
solutionReview.commonError: Starting the quotient with x³: the quotient is one degree lower than the dividend.

questions.prompt: Use synthetic division to find $(x^3 - 7x + 6) \div (x + 3)$. One power of $x$ is missing.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Two things to watch: x + 3 means r = −3, and a missing power needs a 0 in its place.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Divide (x³ − 3x − 2) ÷ (x + 1) by synthetic division. r = −1 → Coefficients 1, 0, −3, −2 → Bring down 1; 1 · (−1) = −1, and 0 + (−1) = −1 → −1 · (−1) = 1, and −3 + 1 = −2 → −2 · (−1) = 2, and −2 + 2 = 0 → Quotient x² − x − 2

hints: x + 3 is x − (−3). What is r?
The dividend has no x² term. Write 0 for its coefficient.
Multiplying by a negative r changes the sign of each product.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which list of coefficients stands for x³ − 7x + 6?

solutionReview.headline: r = −3, with a 0 for the missing x².
reasoning: The bottom row 1, −3, 2 gives the quotient x² − 3x + 2.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving out the 0 for the missing x² term, which puts every number in the wrong column.

questions.prompt: Let $P(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 4x + 12$. Find $P(1)$, then decide whether $x - 1$ is a factor of $P(x)$.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Remainder Theorem: P(r) is the remainder when P(x) is divided by x − r. Factor Theorem: x − r is a factor exactly when P(r) = 0.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: For P(x) = x³ + x² − 4x + 1, find P(2). Is x − 2 a factor? P(2) = 2³ + 2² − 4(2) + 1 → 8 + 4 − 8 + 1 = 5 → The remainder of P(x) ÷ (x − 2) is 5 → x − 2 is not a factor

hints: Put 1 in place of every x in the polynomial.
Any power of 1 is 1, so the terms are 1, −3, −4 and 12.
Is your value of P(1) zero? Only then is x − 1 a factor.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. x − r is a factor of P(x) when P(r) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Evaluate, then compare with 0.
reasoning: P(1) is not 0, so dividing by x − 1 leaves a remainder of 6.
solutionReview.answerSummary: P(1) = 6, so x − 1 is not a factor
solutionReview.commonError: Calling x − 1 a factor because P(1) came out a whole number: only a value of 0 makes it a factor.

questions.prompt: Let $P(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 4x + 12$. Use synthetic division to find $P(3)$, then decide whether $x - 3$ is a factor.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: The last number of a synthetic division by x − r is the remainder, and the remainder is P(r). So the table finds P(r) without powers.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Use synthetic division to find P(1) for P(x) = x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6. Is x − 1 a factor? r = 1; coefficients 1, −6, 11, −6 → Bring down 1; 1 · 1 = 1, and −6 + 1 = −5 → −5 · 1 = −5, and 11 − 5 = 6 → 6 · 1 = 6, and −6 + 6 = 0 → P(1) = 0, so x − 1 is a factor → P(x) = (x − 1)(x² − 5x + 6)

hints: Put 3 in the corner and write the coefficients 1, −3, −4, 12.
Bring down, multiply by 3, add. Do it for every column.
The last number of the bottom row is P(3). What does it tell you about x − 3?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In synthetic division, the last number of the bottom row is the…

solutionReview.headline: The table’s last number is P(3).
solutionReview.answerSummary: P(3) = 0, so x − 3 is a factor
solutionReview.commonError: Reading the first number of the bottom row as P(3): the value is the last number.

questions.prompt: Let $P(x) = x^3 + 4x^2 + x - 6$. Use synthetic division with $x + 2$ to find $P(-2)$ and the quotient. Then decide whether $x + 2$ is a factor.
hints: x + 2 is x − (−2), so −2 goes in the corner.
Multiplying by −2 changes the sign of each product. Add each column carefully.
The last number is P(−2). The numbers before it are the coefficients of the quotient, which starts with x².

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For the divisor x + 2, the number in the corner is…

solutionReview.headline: One table gives the value, the quotient and the answer about the factor.
reasoning: The bottom row 1, 2, −3 gives the quotient, so P(x) = (x + 2)(x² + 2x − 3).
solutionReview.answerSummary: P(−2) = 0; the quotient is x² + 2x − 3; x + 2 is a factor
solutionReview.commonError: Using 2 in the corner: the divisor x + 2 is zero at x = −2.

questions.prompt: Factor $6x^3 + 9x^2$ by taking out the greatest common factor (GCF).

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: The GCF is the largest number and the lowest power of the variable that every term has. Factoring it out is the first step of every factoring problem.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Factor 8x³ + 12x. The GCF of 8 and 12 is 4 → The GCF of x³ and x is x → 8x³ ÷ 4x = 2x² and 12x ÷ 4x = 3 → 4x(2x² + 3) → 4x · 2x² + 4x · 3 = 8x³ + 12x

hints: What is the largest number that divides both 6 and 9?
Both terms have x. Take the lower power.
Divide each term by the GCF to find what stays inside the parentheses.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. x³ ÷ x² equals…

solutionReview.headline: Find the GCF, divide, write the product.
reasoning: The GCF of 6 and 9 is 3, and the lower power of x is x², so the GCF is 3x².
solutionReview.commonError: Taking out only 3 or only x²: the GCF has both the number and the variable part.

questions.prompt: Factor $x^2 + 7x + 12$. Find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: x² + bx + c = (x + p)(x + q) when p · q = c and p + q = b. List the factor pairs of c and look at their sums.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Factor x² + 8x + 15. Find two numbers that multiply to 15 and add to 8 → Pairs for 15: 1 and 15 (sum 16), 3 and 5 (sum 8) → (x + 3)(x + 5) → x² + 5x + 3x + 15 = x² + 8x + 15

hints: List the pairs of whole numbers that multiply to 12.
Add each pair. Which pair has a sum of 7?
Both numbers are positive here, because the product and the sum are both positive.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which pair multiplies to 12?

solutionReview.headline: Factor pairs of 12 and their sums.
solutionReview.commonError: Choosing 2 and 6 because they multiply to 12: the pair also has to add to 7.

questions.prompt: Factor $x^2 - 2x - 15$. Find two numbers that multiply to $-15$ and add to $-2$.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: When c is negative, the two numbers have opposite signs. The one with the larger size takes the sign of b.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Factor x² − 3x − 10. Find two numbers that multiply to −10 and add to −3 → Pairs: 1 and −10 (sum −9), −1 and 10 (9), 2 and −5 (−3), −2 and 5 (3) → (x + 2)(x − 5) → x² − 5x + 2x − 10 = x² − 3x − 10

hints: A negative product means one number is positive and the other is negative.
Try each factor pair of 15 with one of its two numbers negative.
The sum is negative, so the larger of the two numbers is the negative one.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Two numbers multiply to −15. Their signs are…

solutionReview.headline: Opposite signs, sum −2.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing (x − 3)(x + 5): that multiplies out to x² + 2x − 15, with the wrong sign on the middle term.

questions.prompt: Factor $x^2 - 49$. Its middle term is $0x$, so find two numbers that multiply to $-49$ and add to 0.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: A difference of two squares, a² − b², factors as (a + b)(a − b). The two numbers are opposites, so the middle terms cancel.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Factor x² − 36. x² − 36 = x² + 0x − 36 → Find two numbers that multiply to −36 and add to 0 → 6 and −6 → (x + 6)(x − 6) → x² − 6x + 6x − 36 = x² − 36

hints: Two numbers that add to 0 are opposites, like 4 and −4.
Which number times itself is 49?
Use that number once as a positive and once as a negative.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Two numbers add to 0. They are…

solutionReview.headline: Opposites that multiply to −49.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing (x − 7)(x − 7): that is x² − 14x + 49, a perfect square trinomial, not a difference of squares.

questions.prompt: Read the structure before you factor. Sort each polynomial by the method that factors it.

categories.label: Trinomial: two numbers with a product and a sum
Sum or difference of two cubes

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Count the terms and look at their shape: a shared factor, two squares with a minus, three terms, or two cubes.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Name the method that factors each one: 3x² + 12x, x² − 81, x² + 6x + 8 and x³ − 27. 3x² + 12x: common factor → x² − 81: difference of two squares → x² + 6x + 8: trinomial → x³ − 27: difference of two cubes

hints: Count the terms first. Three terms with x² first is a trinomial.
Two terms with a minus sign: are both perfect squares, or both perfect cubes?
If every term shares a number or an x, and nothing else works afterward, it is a common factor only.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. How many terms does a trinomial have?

solutionReview.headline: Count the terms, then look at the shape.
reasoning: Difference of two squares: x² − 36 = x² − 6² and 4x² − 9 = (2x)² − 3².
Trinomial: x² + 9x + 20 and x² − 4x − 12 each have three terms.
solutionReview.answerSummary: GCF: 5x² + 10x, 7x³ − 21x. Squares: x² − 36, 4x² − 9. Trinomial: x² + 9x + 20, x² − 4x − 12. Cubes: x³ + 8, 27x³ − 1
solutionReview.commonError: Putting x³ + 8 with the squares: 8 is 2³, a cube, and a sum of squares would not factor anyway.

questions.prompt: Factor $3x^2 + 8x + 4$ with the $ac$ method, one step at a time.

responses.label: Two numbers multiply to a · c and add to 8. The smaller one is
Split and group: 3x² + 2x + 6x + 4 = x(3x + 2) + 2(3x + 2). The binomial both groups share is

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: When a is not 1: multiply a · c, find the pair that multiplies to a · c and adds to b, split the middle term, then factor by grouping.

hints: Here a = 3, b = 8 and c = 4.
List the pairs that multiply to a · c and add each pair.
After you split 8x into two terms, factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In 3x² + 8x + 4, the value of a is…

solutionReview.headline: a · c, pair, split, group.
reasoning: a · c = 3 · 4 = 12. The pair 2 and 6 multiplies to 12 and adds to 8.
solutionReview.commonError: Using the pair for c alone, 2 and 2, and writing (x + 2)(x + 2): with a = 3 the pair must multiply to a · c.

questions.prompt: Factor $2x^4 + 16x$ completely. Take out the GCF first, then factor the sum of two cubes.

responses.label: After the GCF comes out, what is left in the parentheses?
x³ + 8 = a³ + b³ with a = x. The value of b is
Use a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²). x³ + 8 =

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: Factor completely: GCF first, then look at what is left. Two perfect cubes follow a³ ± b³ = (a ± b)(a² ∓ ab + b²).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.instruction: Factor 3x⁴ − 81x completely. 3x(x³ − 27) → x³ − 27 = x³ − 3³ → a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) → x³ − 27 = (x − 3)(x² + 3x + 9) → 3x(x − 3)(x² + 3x + 9)

hints: Both terms share a number and an x. Take the largest of each.
What is left has two terms. Is 8 a perfect cube?
In the pattern, the binomial keeps the plus sign and the middle term of the trinomial is negative.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which of these is a perfect cube?

solutionReview.headline: GCF, then the sum of cubes.
reasoning: x³ + 8 = x³ + 2³, a sum of cubes with a = x and b = 2.
a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) gives (x + 2)(x² − 2x + 4).
solutionReview.commonError: Writing the trinomial as x² + 2x + 4: in a sum of cubes the middle term of the trinomial is negative.

sections.title: Unit 9 — nth roots and operations with radical expressions

questions.prompt: Find the value of each root. Then sort the cards by their value.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.instruction: The index tells how many equal factors to look for. An odd index can have a negative answer; an even index cannot take a negative radicand.

hints: The small number on the root is the index. ∛ asks: what number, used as a factor 3 times, makes the radicand?
For a negative radicand, check the index. Is it even or odd?
An even number of equal factors can never multiply to a negative number.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (−2)(−2)(−2) equals…
